The record:
Write the overview of the executive synopsis for the incident on io-shop below: a short paragraph in plain words, for the people who lead the company rather than the engineers who responded - what happened, how long it lasted, what it cost the business and the people who responded, and how it was resolved.

What a reader saw: Shop pages slowed sharply for shoppers
Why, in plain words: The shop got far more requests than usual, more than its servers had the computing power to handle at once, so requests had to wait their turn.

Figures:
- How long it lasted: 8m 57s {duration}
- What it cost the shop in takings (estimated by Argus): none {customer_loss}
- Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one.

What was done to end it:
- Argus: scaled out the deployment of io-shop - confirmed, still in place - automatic sync left off
- Argus: proposed a fix, PR #529 - opened as a draft

Name {duration} and {customer_loss} in your overview.
Write no figure yourself - not in digits, not spelled out, and not as a word that sizes it ("a brief outage", "a minor loss", "tripled"). Where a figure goes, write its name, braces and all, and the synopsis writes the figure in.
Say nothing about how the incident was resolved beyond what the list of what was done says: a draft fix has not run, and nothing it would do has happened.
Speak of Argus by name, never as "we", "our" or "us": Argus is the system that responded, and each line of what was done says who did it.
Where you say who was affected, say which ones, as the cause does, or that some were, where it does not say which - never how many, and never all of them, where the cause does not say all.
Keep "likely" on what the cause says is likely, and only there.

Call submit_executive_overview with your overview.

The postmortem it is written from:
Shop pages slowed sharply for shoppers
Incident: HighLatency on io-shop
Date: Nov 11, 2026, 02:08 to 02:16:57 UTC
Status: Draft. 1 of 7 action items are done.
Written by: Argus Postmortem agent, Nov 11, 2026, 02:40:30 UTC. Not reviewed yet. Each part is as of when the work it reports ended, which the timeline dates; who ended the incident is as of now.
First told: Argus posted in Slack, Nov 11, 2026, 02:16:29 UTC
Ended by: Argus: scaled out the deployment of io-shop - confirmed, still in place

Summary
The service broke at 02:08 UTC and was back to normal at 02:16:57 UTC, 8 minutes 57 seconds later. What its alert watches went from 214 ms before it began to 1811 ms at its worst. The shop's takings fell short of the same hours on earlier weeks by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all. The shop got far more requests than usual, more than its servers had the computing power to handle at once, so requests had to wait their turn. What Argus did: scaled out the deployment of io-shop (can be put back) - confirmed, still in place. Argus opened a draft fix, PR #529, for a person to review and merge. Argus left automatic sync of io-shop off, to be turned back on once its repository says what should run (AI-3). If requests rise beyond what the scaled-out replicas' CPU can handle, io-shop could run out of CPU again and slow down the same way.

Impact
8m 57s - onset until back to normal
1.1% to 1.1% - error rate, before onset and while broken on average (no rise)
214 ms to 1315 ms - what the alert watches, before onset and while broken on average (worst minute 1811 ms; the rule's line is 600 ms)
none - customer loss (estimated)

Root cause and contributing factors
Requests to io-shop climbed from 1200/min to as high as 5400/min, and CPU use climbed with them until it reached the service's CPU limit (100.0% at its highest). From then on the replicas had more work than CPU to do it, so requests waited for CPU and responses slowed.
Causal chain
symptom Responses from io-shop slowed sharply. The time within which nearly all requests are answered rose far above its usual level, so shoppers waited much longer for pages.
  Evidence:
    AL1 p95 latency above threshold for 5m
why 1 Requests were waiting for CPU: the service was using all of the CPU its limit allowed.
  Evidence:
    R2 CPU in use, as a share of the service's CPU limit: 25.0% before it began, 94.7% on average while it was broken, 100.0% at its highest.
why 2 CPU use reached that limit because requests rose to several times their level before the onset and CPU use rose in step with them. That was more load than the replicas' CPU could handle.
  Evidence:
    R1 Requests: 1200/min before it began, 4841/min on average while it was broken, 5400/min at its highest.
    R2
  Ruled out:
    A deploy, release or flag change on the service: the Investigator Agent asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 day 1 minute before Nov 11 02:09; the Investigator Agent read back 0 production changes.
      T7
      T8
    A flag change by anyone but Argus: Argus read the flag provider's history - 0 flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 02:16:52.
      T12
    A rollout still under way: the Investigator Agent read how far the deployment had rolled out - all 3 replicas run one revision, which the history does not name.
      T9
Contributing factors
- No replicas were seen being added automatically as CPU use reached its limit. The service stayed at 3 replicas until Argus scaled it out. (AI-4)
- Each request likely cost more CPU than it needed to. Code-Fix read the files behind the account page's spending figures: the default figure, and the one behind typical-purchase-feature, both do work that grows with the square of a shopper's purchase history. Nothing has run this reading. (AI-2)
- No alert was seen when CPU use neared its limit. The slowdown was found only by the latency alert, which waits 5 minutes with its condition holding before it fires. (AI-5)

Hypotheses considered
 | Hypothesis | Confidence | Result
C1 | Request volume ramped from 1200/min starting 02:03 UTC to 5400/min, about 4.5 times baseline. CPU use rose with it and hit the fixed 3.0-core limit at 02:11 UTC. Requests then queued for CPU, and p95 rose from about 210 ms to over 1800 ms. Nothing was deployed or changed, and the rollout had converged. | 0.85 | confirmed

Trigger
C1 was confirmed; it blames io-shop itself and names no change to it.

Resolution
 | Time (UTC) | Action | By | Kind | Outcome
M1 | 02:16:57 | Scaled out the deployment of io-shop for C1 | Argus | can be put back | confirmed, still in place - automatic sync left off
 | 02:20:34 | Proposed a fix: PR #529 | Code-Fix Agent | nothing to put back | opened as a draft

Detection
The incident on io-shop began at 02:08 UTC. HighLatency fired at 02:16:07 UTC, 8 minutes 7 seconds later.
What the alert said
AL1 | p95 latency above threshold for 5m

Action items
Item | Action | Type | Owner | Tracking | Status
AI-1 | Scaled out the deployment of io-shop | mitigate | Argus | - | done
AI-2 | Review and merge the proposed fix | prevent | unassigned | PR #529 | open
AI-3 | Turn automatic sync of io-shop back on once its repository says what should run - until then nothing merged reaches it, and turned on sooner it puts back what the repository says, undoing what Argus changed by hand | mitigate | unassigned | - | open
AI-4 | Configure io-shop to add replicas automatically as CPU use nears its limit, with enough room for at least the peak request rate seen in this incident (5400/min). | prevent | unassigned | - | open
AI-5 | Add an alert on io-shop's CPU use as a share of its CPU limit, so the service is flagged when it nears saturation and before latency climbs. | detect | unassigned | - | open
AI-6 | Make the HighLatency alert on io-shop page the on-call engineer. | process | unassigned | - | open
AI-7 | Find where the rise in requests to io-shop came from, and whether it can happen again at this size or larger. | process | unassigned | - | open

Lessons learned
What went well
- The alert came 7 minutes 7 seconds after its series passed its line, within the 7 minutes 30 seconds accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute its series is read in.
- 44 seconds after the alert was raised, the Investigator Agent read back 0 production changes.
- 50 seconds after the alert was raised, the Mitigation Agent scaled out the deployment of io-shop for C1.
- 2 minutes 54 seconds after the alert was raised, the Mitigation Agent judged the action CONFIRMED.
- 4 minutes 27 seconds after the alert was raised, the Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as a draft pull request - PR #529.
What went wrong
- Nobody was paged: the alert did not open an on-call incident.
Where it got lucky
Nothing.

Timeline (UTC)
 | Nov 11 02:08 | IMPACT BEGINS | the incident began
 | 02:16:07 | DETECTED | HighLatency on io-shop fired
T1 | 02:16:28 |  | Argus Received HighLatency on io-shop
T2 | 02:16:36 |  | Argus Moved the incident to INVESTIGATING - a worker took the incident up
T3 | 02:16:43 |  | Investigator Agent Asked for the service's per-minute metrics, anchored on 02:16:07
T4 | 02:16:47 |  | Investigator Agent Read back 360 minutes of metrics
T5 | 02:16:49 |  | Investigator Agent Placed the start of the incident at 02:08
T6 | 02:16:49 |  | Investigator Agent Recorded where the 3 replicas run - all on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB
T7 | 02:16:50 |  | Investigator Agent Asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 day 1 minute before Nov 11 02:09
T8 | 02:16:51 |  | Investigator Agent Read back 0 production changes
T9 | 02:16:51 |  | Investigator Agent Read how far the deployment had rolled out - all 3 replicas run one revision, which the history does not name
T10 | 02:16:52 |  | Investigator Agent Formed 1 candidate cause, best first: C1
T11 | 02:16:52 |  | Investigator Agent Did not read logs
T12 | 02:16:52 |  | Argus Read the flag provider's history - 0 flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 02:16:52
T13 | 02:16:56 |  | Argus Moved the incident to MITIGATING to act on a candidate
T14 | 02:16:57 | MITIGATION APPLIED | Mitigation Agent Scaled out the deployment of io-shop for C1
 | 02:16:57 | IMPACT ENDS | the service was back to normal
T15 | 02:17:04 |  | Mitigation Agent Waiting to see whether the service is still at the incident's level, from 02:17 - up to 182s
T16 | 02:19:01 |  | Mitigation Agent Looked at the service - no longer at the incident's level since 02:16
T17 | 02:19:01 |  | Mitigation Agent Judged the action CONFIRMED
T18 | 02:19:01 |  | Argus Moved the incident to MITIGATED - scaled io-shop out from 3 replicas and the rule that fired stopped firing
T19 | 02:20:34 |  | Code-Fix Agent Proposed a fix as a draft pull request - PR #529

Response effort
none - engineer time
171,298 - tokens spent by Argus

Supporting information
The incident's walk: http://localhost:8000/incidents/c9367f0f-0459-4f4a-be1b-00cacfa883f7
The fix it proposed: PR #529 (https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/529) opened as a draft. The record holds nothing about it after that.
Changes to production read
Deploys read, none came back; flags read, none came back.
Log messages read (UTC)
Not read.
What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed - nothing ran its test or its fix
F1 | The investigation found CPU rising in step with request volume until it hit the fixed 3.0-core limit, and nothing deployed or changed. That makes CPU cost per request the thing this code controls. Both functions in the account page's figure path do quadratic work for each request:

• average_spend_per_item in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py is the default figure, rendered for every request outside the rollouts. For each purchase it re-sums the whole prefix account.purchases[:index + 1], then throws away every sum except the last. That is n(n+1)/2 price reads plus n slice copies to get one total, which a single sum over the purchases gives. The fix sums once. The result is unchanged: it is still derived from the purchases, not from the carried total_cents. An empty history still raises ZeroDivisionError (0 // 0), which the existing boundary test relies on.
• typical_spend_per_item in src/io_shop/typical_spend.py (behind typical-purchase-feature) runs min and remove over the remaining list about n/2 times, which is also O(n²). The fix sorts once and indexes the lower middle, (n - 1) // 2. That picks the same element the old loop did, including repeated prices and the lower middle of an even-length history. An empty history still raises ValueError, as the old min([]) did.

The more history a shopper has, the faster per-request cost grew, so the pods hit the CPU limit at a much lower request rate than the work needs. This change doesn't remove the fixed limit or the autoscaling settings in deploy/values-production.yaml. It cuts how much CPU each page costs, so the same cores serve more requests before they queue. Nothing has run these changes or the tests; the claims below come from reading the code.

Tests:
• tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py adds a case that counts reads of price_cents over a 1000-purchase history and asserts at most 2n. The old prefix re-summing does about 500,000 reads.
• tests/io_shop/test_typical_spend.py adds a case that counts < comparisons between prices over a shuffled 1000-purchase history and asserts fewer than 50,000. A single sort needs about n log n (roughly 10,000); the old repeated min needs several hundred thousand. Both new tests also check that the answer is still right, and the existing correctness tests are kept unchanged.
What the metrics show of the confirmed cause, measured by Argus
R1 | Requests: 1200/min before it began, 4841/min on average while it was broken, 5400/min at its highest.
R2 | CPU in use, as a share of the service's CPU limit: 25.0% before it began, 94.7% on average while it was broken, 100.0% at its highest.
Assumptions
- Exchange rate: EUR converted at 0.92191 per USD, published 2026-11-10
- No engineer minutes: no on-call incident was linked to this one, so nobody was paged to respond

Review checklist
✓ Key incident data collected (met)
✓ Impact assessed (met)
✓ Root-cause analysis complete (met)
○ Every action item owned and dated (for a person)
○ Reviewed and shared (for a person)

The document, by field:
overview: For {duration}, io-shop pages slowed for some shoppers. The shop received more requests than its servers had the computing power to handle at once, so requests had to wait their turn. Argus estimates the lost takings at {customer_loss}. Nobody was paged, and no on-call incident was linked to this one. Argus ended the slowdown by scaling out io-shop's deployment to add capacity. That change has been confirmed and is still in place, with automatic sync left off. Argus also proposed a longer-term fix, which is still a draft and has not been applied.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {duration}, are figures code writes in from the list of figures in the ask. They are not judged.
  - The overview is written in plain words for the people who lead the company. A claim said more plainly than the postmortem says it is grounded where it means the same.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
